title: No. 71 — The Duration in Office of the Executive (Hamilton)
paragraphs: Duration in office has been mentioned as the second requirement for energy in the Executive authority. This has to do with two objects: the personal firmness of the executive magistrate in exercising his constitutional powers, and the stability of the system of administration adopted under his leadership. As to the first, it must be evident that the longer the term in office, the greater the chance of securing this important advantage. It is a general principle of human nature that a man's interest in what he holds is proportional to how firm or precarious his hold is. He will be less attached to what he holds by a momentary or uncertain title than to what he enjoys by a durable or certain one. He will, of course, be willing to risk more for the sake of the latter than the former. This observation applies just as much to a political privilege, honor, or trust as to any ordinary piece of property. The conclusion is that a man acting as chief magistrate, conscious that in a very short time he MUST leave office, will likely feel too little interested in it to risk any serious censure or trouble by an independent exercise of his powers, or by confronting the ill humors — however brief — that may prevail in a considerable part of society itself, or even in a dominant faction of the legislature. If the case is only that he MIGHT leave it unless continued by a new election, and if he wishes to be continued, his hopes — combined with his fears — would tend even more powerfully to corrupt his integrity or weaken his courage. In either case, feebleness and irresolution must mark the office.

There are some who would be inclined to view the servile pliancy of the Executive to a prevailing current — either in the community or in the legislature — as its chief recommendation. But such people hold very crude notions both of the purposes for which government was instituted and of the true means by which public happiness can be promoted. The republican principle requires that the deliberate sense of the community should govern the conduct of those entrusted with managing its affairs. But it does not require unqualified compliance with every sudden gust of passion, or every transient impulse the people may receive from the arts of those who flatter their prejudices in order to betray their interests. It is a fair observation that the people commonly INTEND the PUBLIC GOOD. This often applies even to their errors. But their good sense would scorn the flatterer who pretended that they always REASON RIGHT about the MEANS of promoting it. They know from experience that they sometimes err. The wonder is that they err so seldom, surrounded as they continually are by the wiles of parasites and sycophants, by the snares of the ambitious, the avaricious, the desperate, by the tricks of men who have their confidence more than they deserve it, and of those who seek to possess rather than deserve it. When occasions arise in which the interests of the people clash with their inclinations, it is the duty of the persons appointed to be the guardians of those interests to withstand the temporary delusion — to give the people time and opportunity for cooler and more sedate reflection. Instances could be cited in which conduct of this kind has saved the people from very fatal consequences of their own mistakes, and has earned lasting monuments of their gratitude toward the men who had courage and magnanimity enough to serve them at the risk of their displeasure.

But however inclined we might be to insist on unbounded compliance by the Executive with the inclinations of the people, we cannot reasonably argue for similar compliance with the moods of the legislature. The legislature may sometimes stand in opposition to the people, and at other times the people may be entirely neutral. In either case, it is surely desirable that the Executive be in a position to dare to act on his own opinion with vigor and decision.

The same rule that teaches the propriety of partitioning the various branches of power also teaches that this partition ought to be designed so that each is independent of the other. What is the point of separating the executive or the judiciary from the legislature, if both the executive and the judiciary are so constituted as to be entirely at the legislature's mercy? Such a separation must be merely nominal, and incapable of achieving its purpose. It is one thing to be subordinate to the laws, and another to be dependent on the legislative body. The first agrees with, the second violates, the fundamental principles of good government. Whatever the forms of the Constitution, the second arrangement unites all power in the same hands. The tendency of the legislative authority to absorb every other has been fully displayed and illustrated by examples in some preceding numbers. In purely republican governments, this tendency is almost irresistible. The representatives of the people in a popular assembly sometimes seem to imagine that they are the people themselves, and they betray strong symptoms of impatience and disgust at the slightest sign of opposition from any other quarter — as if the exercise of its rights by either the executive or the judiciary were a breach of their privilege and an outrage to their dignity. They often appear disposed to exert imperious control over the other departments. And as they commonly have the people on their side, they always act with such momentum that it becomes very difficult for the other branches of the government to maintain the balance of the Constitution.

It may be asked how the shortness of duration in office can affect the Executive's independence of the legislature, unless one had the power of appointing or removing the other. One answer to this question can be drawn from the principle already noted: the slight interest a man tends to take in a short-lived advantage, and the small inducement it gives him to expose himself, on its account, to any considerable inconvenience or risk. Another answer, perhaps more obvious though not more conclusive, will arise from considering the legislative body's influence over the people. That influence might be used to prevent the re-election of a man who, by upright resistance to some sinister project of the legislature, has made himself obnoxious to its resentment.

It may also be asked whether a duration of four years would answer the proposed end. And if it would not, whether a shorter period — which would at least be recommended by greater security against ambitious designs — would not, for that reason, be preferable to a longer period that was at the same time still too short to inspire the desired firmness and independence in the magistrate.

It cannot be claimed that a duration of four years, or any other limited term, would completely achieve the proposed end. But it would contribute toward it to a degree that would materially shape the spirit and character of the government. Between the start and end of such a period there would always be a considerable interval in which the prospect of leaving office would be remote enough not to have an improper effect on the conduct of a man with even a moderate share of fortitude. He might reasonably promise himself that there would be time enough before that moment arrived to make the community appreciate the soundness of the measures he was inclined to pursue. Though it is probable that, as he approached the moment when the public would, by a new election, signify their judgment of his conduct, his confidence — and with it his firmness — would decline, both would still draw support from the opportunities his prior continuance in office had given him to establish himself in the esteem and good will of his constituents. He could then take risks with safety, in proportion to the proofs he had given of his wisdom and integrity, and to the claim he had acquired to the respect and attachment of his fellow citizens. On the one hand, a four-year term will contribute to the firmness of the Executive enough to make it a very valuable ingredient in its composition. On the other, it is not enough to justify any alarm for public liberty. If a British House of Commons, from the most feeble beginnings — FROM THE MERE POWER OF ASSENTING TO OR DISAGREEING WITH THE IMPOSITION OF A NEW TAX — has, by rapid strides, reduced the prerogatives of the crown and the privileges of the nobility within limits they considered compatible with the principles of free government, while raising itself to the rank and consequence of a coequal branch of the legislature; if it has been able in one instance to abolish both the royalty and the aristocracy, and to overturn all the ancient establishments, as well in Church as in State; if it has been able, on a recent occasion, to make the monarch tremble at the prospect of an innovation(1) attempted by it — what is to be feared from an elective magistrate of four years' duration, with the limited authorities of a President of the United States? What, except that he might be unequal to the task the Constitution assigns him? I will only add that if his term is so short as to leave doubt about his firmness, that doubt is inconsistent with a jealousy of his encroachments.
1. This was the case with respect to Mr. Fox's India bill, which was carried in the House of Commons and rejected in the House of Lords, to the entire satisfaction, it is said, of the people.
